cdn_women_gender.label: Canadian women's & gender history
cdn_women_gender.date_label: Earlier women writers of history (recovered by Boutilier and Prentice 1997) and Cleverdon’s suffrage history 1950 · collections and studies 1976–79 · Collectif Clio 1982 · Prentice et al. 1988 · Parr 1990 · Left History exchange 1995–96 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
cdn_women_gender.description: Canadian women's history studies women as historical actors in Canada and, increasingly from the 1990s, gender as a relation shaping work, family, politics, law and the state. Earlier women wrote national, local and regional history, recovered by Boutilier and Prentice (1997); Cleverdon studied the suffrage movement (1950); collections and studies of reform and women's organizations followed in the later 1970s (Cook and Mitchinson; Strong-Boag; Kealey). Two syntheses had different starting points. The Collectif Clio's L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982) rejected a male-centred history presented as everyone's history; Prentice and colleagues' Canadian Women: A History (1988) offered a collaborative survey. Studies of women and war (Pierson), women on the left (Sangster), working families in Montreal (Bradbury) and housewives in the Depression (Baillargeon) joined the field to labour and family history. Parr's comparison of two Ontario towns (1990) challenged assumptions about the separateness of gender and class roles. In the 1990s historians argued over whether gender history extended or displaced women's history: Pierson weighed the turn to deconstruction and Scott's theory of gender against experience and voice (1991), and Sangster's 'Beyond Dichotomies' (1995), by her later account, protested a hierarchy that set gender history above a 'limited' women's history; replies in Left History defended gender history (1996). Later work examined masculinity and gendered political languages (Morgan), sexuality and the law, and postwar domesticity and consumption (Parr, Korinek, Fahrni). Lévesque asked how far Quebec historiography had integrated women (1997); Quebec women's history is treated mainly under Quebec historiography.
cdn_women_gender.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier women writers of history: Machar, Skinner, Skelton, Esther Clark Wright, Neatby, Ormsby, Daveluy, as recovered in Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Cleverdon, The Woman Suffrage Movement in Canada (1950). Collectif Clio, L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982; Quebec Women, 1987); Prentice et al., Canadian Women: A History (1988). Pierson, "They're Still Women After All" (1986); Danylewycz, Taking the Veil (1987); Strong-Boag, The New Day Recalled (1988); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la crise (1991); Mitchinson, The Nature of Their Bodies (1991); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Dubinsky, Improper Advances (1993). Debate: Pierson (1991); Parr (1995); Sangster (1995, 1996); Iacovetta and Kealey (1996); Dubinsky and Marks (1996); Lévesque (1997); Sangster's retrospect (2011). Morgan, Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996); McPherson, Morgan and Forestell, eds., Gendered Pasts (1999); Parr, Domestic Goods (1999); Korinek, Roughing It in the Suburbs (2000); Christie, Engendering the State (2000). cdn_women_gender.scope_note: A Canadian research field joining women's history and gender history; the entry does not decide the 1990s argument between them. Quebec women's history (Collectif Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) has its primary treatment in Quebec historiography; this entry keeps those authors' work on family, work and sexuality and a critique edge to Quebec historiography. Fur-trade women (Van Kirk) and gender and empire (Perry) are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism and appear here as comparison rows; sexuality, law and regulation overlap with Moral regulation; childhood and family with Childhood, youth & family in Canada. Palmer's Descent into Discourse is treated in Canadian working-class history, as a critique of the linguistic turn, not of women's history.

strands.title: Earlier women writers of history
strands.focus: Women wrote Canadian history long before women’s history was a field: popular, local and regional historians (Machar, Skinner, Esther Clark Wright), the independent scholar Isabel Skelton, and a few university historians, among them Hilda Neatby and Margaret Ormsby, the CHA’s first and second women presidents (1962–63; 1965–66). In French Canada, Marie-Claire Daveluy wrote on New France. Most wrote national, local, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (who “sought to write women back into Canadian history”, per Coulter’s reading of Crowley) and Daveluy (Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women in. They are earlier women writers of history, not founders of women’s history. Boutilier and Prentice’s Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalization masculinized history; the editors note that their subjects come mainly from “the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society”. Cleverdon’s suffrage history (1950) is the earlier study of women that PhDs still cite. Bienvenue and Dorais (2023) extend the recovery to French Canada (after 2000).
strands.works: Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Prentice, “Laying Siege to the History Professoriate” (1997); Cleverdon (1950); Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018)

native_newcomer.label: Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history
native_newcomer.date_label: Earlier resources: Innis 1930, Stanley 1936 · Ray 1974 · Van Kirk and Brown 1980 · Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers 1985 · Miller 1989 · Milloy 1999 · selected later works
native_newcomer.description: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and European newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis’s Fur Trade in Canada (1930) was subtitled ‘an introduction to Canadian economic history’. From the 1970s historians, geographers and archaeologists recast it with Indigenous people as actors: trappers, hunters and middlemen (Ray 1974), wives and kin in fur-trade society (Van Kirk; Brown, both 1980), and Wendat history across contact (Trigger 1976, 1985; Delâge 1985), while Dickason studied European representations of them (1984). The field long called itself ‘native–newcomer’ history, after Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985); current usage prefers ‘Indigenous’. Miller (1989) offered a national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’. Later work studied reserve farming and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), health (Kelm 1998) and wage labour (Lutz 1992). Brownlie and Kelm (1994) asked whether agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin; Miller; Loo) had made Native agency a colonialist alibi. Indigenous scholars questioned the framing: Sioui (1989) found conventional history without a method for Indigenous self-interpretation; Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (1998) argued that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and set oral history aside; LaRocque (1999) found that the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk still ‘othered’ its subjects. After 2000, settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession; Greer replied that the fur trade’s commercial penetration was a different form of invasion.
native_newcomer.representative_figures_and_works: Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada (1930); Stanley, The Birth of Western Canada (1936); Ray, Indians in the Fur Trade (1974); Fisher, Contact and Conflict (1977); Van Kirk, “Many Tender Ties” (1980); Brown, Strangers in Blood (1980); Trigger, The Children of Aataentsic (1976), Natives and Newcomers (1985), “The Historians’ Indian” (1986); Delâge, Le pays renversé (1985); Dickason, The Myth of the Savage (1984), Canada’s First Nations (1992); Smith, Sacred Feathers (1987); Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989), Shingwauk’s Vision (1996); Carter, Lost Harvests (1990); Coates, Best Left as Indians (1991); Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Brownlie and Kelm, “Desperately Seeking Absolution” (1994); Kelm, Colonizing Bodies (1998); Milloy, “A National Crime” (1999). Later: Rutherdale (2002), Brownlie (2003), Raibmon (2005), Podruchny (2006), Lutz, Makúk (2008). Critics and alternatives: Sioui (1989), Paul, We Were Not the Savages (1993; 2000 edition), Stevenson [Wheeler], “The Othering of Indigenous History” (1998), LaRocque (1999); in the US, Fixico (2009) and S. A. Miller (2009).
native_newcomer.scope_note: A research field in mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian historiography, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology and anthropology. It is not the atlas’s Indigenous history entry, which centres Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and authority. Several people sit in both (Dickason, Miller, Lutz, Trigger); their existing contexts are kept, and Indigenous historical practice is not subsumed here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure: most works here predate that framework, and whether any adopts it was not checked; and Greer’s critique points the other way. Indigenous critiques of the ‘relations’ framing (Sioui, LaRocque; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. Francophone work is thin in this selection (Delâge, Sioui); New France encounter history overlaps with Quebec historiography. The label keeps the field’s word ‘newcomer’ but uses ‘Indigenous’; ‘native–newcomer’, Trigger’s 1985 term, is explained in the description as the field’s historical name. ‘Indigenous–settler’ is avoided so as not to collide with Settler colonialism.

strands.title: Indigenous critiques of the relations frame
strands.focus: Sioui (1989), Stevenson/Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) criticise the relations framing from Indigenous standpoints: its reliance on colonial documents, its disregard of oral history and its ethnological distance. Fixico and S. Miller (2009, US) question ‘Indian–white relations’ as the premise of Indian history. Paul’s We Were Not the Savages (1993; the 2000 Fernwood edition is the one PhDs cite), subtitled ‘a Mi’kmaq perspective’, rejects the ‘savage’ category (title and subtitle only). Adams’s Prison of Grass (1975) is an earlier counter-history of official history, not a critique of this field, and Dickason is a member of the field. Trigger (1986) and Brownlie and Kelm (1994) are non-Indigenous critiques from inside. These are critics and alternatives, not members.
strands.works: Sioui (1989); Paul (1993; 2000 ed.); Stevenson [Wheeler] (Fall 1998); LaRocque (1999); Fixico (2009); S. A. Miller (2009)

strands.title: After 2000: the settler-colonial reading and its critics
strands.focus: Settler-colonial analysis reads reserves, schools and dispossession as a continuing structure. Greer replies that the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others, and that commercial penetration (the fur trade’s mode) and extractivism are other forms of invasion. cdn_regional.label: Canadian regional history
cdn_regional.date_label: Morton's Manitoba 1957 · Ormsby's British Columbia 1958 · Craig's Upper Canada 1963 · 'limited identities' 1967–69 · Acadiensis 1971 · Acheson 1972 · Forbes 1979 · Friesen 1984 · Barman 1991 · reassessments 2000
cdn_regional.description: Histories of Canada's regions as places with their own economies, societies and identities rather than as peripheries of a central-Canadian story. Provincial syntheses such as Morton's Manitoba (1957) and Ormsby's British Columbia (1958) preceded the 'limited identities' argument: Cook (1967) suggested that Canadianism might be found in regional, ethnic and class identities, and Careless (1969) made the phrase a programme. Acadiensis was revived in 1971 (Windsor's initiative; Buckner editor), its first editorial faulting historians 'obsessed with the great "national" themes'. Acheson (1972) traced Maritime industrial growth under the National Policy and its subordination to Montreal capital, and Forbes studied the Maritime Rights movement (1979). Friesen (1984), Barman (1991), Conrad and Hiller (2001) and Waiser (2005) wrote regional syntheses, while Owram, Carter and Harris tied western and Pacific history to expansionist ideas, reserve policy and colonial geography. Ontario had provincial histories of its own (Craig 1963; Nelles 1974; McCalla 1993). Acadia became a growing Atlantic literature: Griffiths on Acadian history and identity (1992, 2005), Plank and Faragher on conquest and expulsion (2001, 2005), and Reid, Basque and colleagues on 1710 (2004). Francophone regional history worked at other scales: Painchaud on the Church and French Prairie settlement (a 1970s study, published posthumously in 1987), Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001), and Quebec's intraprovincial regional histories, which Harvey contrasts with interprovincial regionalism. By 2000 McKay asked whether 'region' could hold the new histories of gender, ethnicity and community, and Buckner revisited limited identities.

Critique: McKay, "A Note on 'Region'" (2000).
cdn_regional.scope_note: A research field for Canada's regions (the Prairie West, British Columbia, the Atlantic provinces including Acadia, and Ontario) and the limited-identities argument. Provincial syntheses, regional economic history, rural history and regional identity are distinct strands. Indigenous and settler-colonial histories of the West and British Columbia overlap strongly (Carter, Harris) and are primarily placed in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history, Settler colonialism and environment. Ontario has a strand of provincial syntheses and economic histories chosen by PhD citation counts; Acadia has its own Atlantic strand. The North and Newfoundland are small in the PhD corpus (about 18 and 9 titles) and get only this note. Quebec's regional history appears only as a contrast of scale. Roster inclusion does not imply that historians accepted "limited identities".

strands.title: Acadia (Atlantic)
strands.focus: Acadia before and after the expulsion of 1755. In the PhD corpus this is a substantial and rising literature: 101 of 1,303 PhDs (2009–2026) cite Acadian history works, 5.1% in 2009–14 and 8.9% in 2020–26, 23 of them at francophone universities. Griffiths, an authority on pre-1755 Acadia, wrote on its contexts to 1784 (1992) and the emergence of Acadian identity (2005); Plank (2001) and Faragher (2005) studied the British campaign against the peoples of Acadia and the expulsion; Reid, Basque and colleagues read the 1710 conquest from imperial, Acadian and Mi'kmaw perspectives (2004). Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001) is a francophone university synthesis of Maritime Acadia over four centuries that sets out to recount the experience of the whole Acadian people, not only its elite. Most of these works are later readings, after 2000. Readers of this literature also engage Quebec historiography (lift 3.2): see the comparison with Quebec historiography.

settler_colonialism.label: Settler colonialism
settler_colonialism.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999, 2006 · journal 2011 · Tuck and Yang 2012 · critiques 2013–14 · TRC 2015 · Wolfe d. 2016 · Englert 2020 · reviewed through 2024
settler_colonialism.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, took land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe gave the field its programme: settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'invasion is a structure not an event' (1999, 2006). Lorenzo Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011) and distinguished colonialism ('you, work for me') from settler colonialism ('you, go away'), adding that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': it 'extinguishes itself'. Two questions organise this selection: how elimination persists while pursuing its own completion, and how settler-colonial analysis relates to Indigenous sovereignty, refusal and resurgence. Veracini develops Wolfe's formula: self-supersession means the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, not a successful decolonisation. The Indigenous reading adopts Wolfe's formula while insisting that 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies' (Kauanui), that 'decolonization is not a metaphor' (Tuck and Yang) and that refusal, not recognition, answers the settler state (Simpson, Coulthard). Settler scholars warn against 'colonial fatalism' (Macoun and Strakosch); Marxists ask whether elimination or exploitation defines the form (Englert). In Canada the frame met an older historiography of reserves, treaties, gender and the state, and the TRC's finding of 'cultural genocide' (2015).

settler_colonialism.scope_note: A research field whose consolidation came after 2000; reviewed through 2024 in the period-4 wave (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md). Read in full: Wolfe 2006 (in an Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page), Veracini 2011 and his 2016 obituary of Wolfe, Kauanui 2016, Englert 2020, Goeman 2016; in most pages, Tuck and Yang 2012 and Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014; Macoun and Strakosch 2013 in the authors' version; Veracini 2013 in its author manuscript (abstract, opening, conclusion); the TRC summary pp. 1–3. Unread, known through publisher pages or named readers: Wolfe 1999 beyond pp. 1–2, 2001, 2008, 2016; Veracini 2010, 2015; Coulthard; A. Simpson (book; 2017 abstract read); Byrd; Moreton-Robinson; L. B. Simpson; Rowse; Konishi; Sexton; Garba and Sorentino; King; Daschuk; Miller 2009; Perry 2015; Carter 2016; McCallum; Mawani; Stanger-Ross; Lowman and Barker; Regan. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies; Veracini (2013) and Kauanui (2016) both record uses of the term before Wolfe (Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973, Denoon 1983, Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis 1995). Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris, Miller, Daschuk and McCallum wrote earlier or beside it, and their publisher descriptions do not use the phrase. Critics appear as critics; Kauanui and Goeman defend Wolfe's theory against shallow citation while asking the field to attend to Indigenous studies. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: two or more of the field's authors are cited by 3.2% of Canada + US theses in 2000–09 and 11.0% in 2020–25 (Canada 15.2%, US 6.8%); Wolfe and Veracini are co-cited by 3.0% of theses in 2020–25 and Wolfe with Tuck and Yang, Simpson or Coulthard by 2.3% (the release's category 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' names a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position: Tuck and Yang build on Wolfe, and Kauanui criticises his reception), the only rising two-sided citing after 2000; the Canadian neighbourhood of the founders is the largest and youngest of any field (51 works, median year 2006), its 2020–25 entrants Coulthard, Simpson, Carter, Miller, Daschuk, Kauanui and Greer. The earlier pilot of 2026-10-12 (Canadian strict History PhDs, 2009–26) found 54 citing a work of Wolfe's and 17 the 1999 book (first in 2012), and Daschuk the work most co-cited with Wolfe and Veracini (19 of 58); these figures say more about Canadian history than about him. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. Francophone uptake in the corpus remains near zero.

strands.title: Structure, not event: the logic of elimination
strands.focus: Wolfe's programme, now read in his own pages. Settler colonialism 'destroys to replace'; it 'is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal'; 'the primary motive for elimination is not race … but access to territory. Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event'; elimination has a 'positive' aspect (allotment, citizenship, child abduction, assimilation) that persists after the frontier, so that the form is 'relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' names its convergence with genocide without 'hierarchy among victims' (2006). The formula goes back to the 1999 book (p. 2) and the 1994 essay (p. 96, per his note 7). Kauanui: the phrase 'often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement of his theory'.

strands.title: Veracini: the field, the journal and the self-superseding structure
strands.focus: Veracini founded Settler Colonial Studies (2011; open access, volunteer-run, on an ARC grant; to Taylor & Francis in 2013) 'to contribute to the consolidation of a new scholarly field'. Colonialism says 'you, work for me'; settler colonialism says 'you, go away'; the two 'should be understood in their dialectical relation'. Developing Wolfe's formula rather than disputing it, he adds that the structure 'persistently pursues a specific end point': 'settler colonialism, by contrast, extinguishes itself' and is 'least visible in the settler cities'. This self-supersession is the settler project's attempted extinction of the settler–Indigenous relation by the disappearance of Indigenous peoples, not a successful decolonisation, which would instead end 'with an indigenous ultimate permanence'; 'decolonisation is not settler decolonisation', and the politics of recognition 'cannot be considered a genuinely decolonising move' (2011). His history of the concept (2013) finds three earlier careers of the term and a consolidation 'from approximately the mid 1990s', with 'both the Canadian and US historiographies … late in adopting' it. Englert calls him Wolfe's 'self-styled intellectual successor'; Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel find in his history 'Indigenous studies and Indigenous resistance … pretty much erased'.

strands.works: Cole Harris, The Resettlement of British Columbia: Essays on Colonialism and Geographical Change (Vancouver: UBC Press, 1997).; Cole Harris, Making Native Space: Colonialism, Resistance, and Reserves in British Columbia (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2002).; Cole Harris, "How Did Colonialism Dispossess? Comments from an Edge of Empire," Annals of the Association of American Geographers 94, no. 1 (2004): 165–182.; Cole Harris, A Bounded Land: Reflections on Settler Colonialism in Canada (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2020).; Sarah Carter, Lost Harvests: Prairie Indian Reserve Farmers and Government Policy (Montreal and Kingston: McGill-Queen's University Press, 1990).

strands.title: Gender, family and colonial nation-making
strands.focus: Gender, race, marriage and child removal in colonial British Columbia, the Prairie West, the American West and Australia. Perry is read in her 1995 and 2001/02 essays and in in-period reviews of On the Edge of Empire, the book itself unread; Carter (2008) and Jacobs (2009) remain at metadata level.
strands.works: Adele Perry, On the Edge of Empire: Gender, Race, and the Making of British Columbia, 1849–1871 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2001).; Sarah Carter, The Importance of Being Monogamous: Marriage and Nation Building in Western Canada to 1915 (Edmonton: University of Alberta Press / Athabasca University Press, 2008).; Margaret D. Jacobs, White Mother to a Dark Race: Settler Colonialism, Maternalism, and the Removal of Indigenous Children in the American West and Australia, 1880–1940 (Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 2009).; Adele Perry, Colonial Relations: The Douglas-Connolly Family and the Nineteenth-Century Imperial World (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2015).; Sarah Carter, Imperial Plots: Women, Land, and the Spadework of British Colonialism on the Canadian Prairies (Winnipeg: University of Manitoba Press, 2016).

strands.title: Settler identity, truth telling and reconciliation
strands.focus: Settler self-examination after residential schools and in contemporary Canada; Regan's contents page names the 'peacemaker myth'. The TRC summary (2015, pp. 1–3 read) finds that residential schools were part of a policy 'which can best be described as "cultural genocide"'; Regan is described by her publisher as the Commission's director of research.
strands.works: Paulette Regan, Unsettling the Settler Within: Indian Residential Schools, Truth Telling, and Reconciliation in Canada (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2010). Foreword by Taiaiake Alfred.; Emma Battell Lowman and Adam J. Barker, Settler: Identity and Colonialism in 21st Century Canada (Halifax and Winnipeg: Fernwood, 2015).; Sherene H. Razack, ed., Race, Space, and the Law: Unmapping a White Settler Society (Toronto: Between the Lines, 2002).

strands.title: Health, starvation and state policy
strands.focus: Daschuk's Plains history is the work most co-cited with Wolfe and Veracini by Canadian History PhDs: 19 of 58 citing theses in the 2026-10-12 pilot (Canadian strict History PhDs, 2009–26), and a 2020–25 entrant to the Canadian settler-colonial neighbourhood (support 12, lift 6.1) in the History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23. Its publisher describes 'a policy of starvation' that 'sparked widespread debate about genocide in Canada' and does not use 'settler colonialism'; the 2019 edition adds responses by Kelm, Mosby, Neylan and Woolford. His own framing remains unchecked; the TRC summary's 'cultural genocide' (2015) is the public text beside which the book is read. A comparison strand.
strands.works: James Daschuk, Clearing the Plains: Disease, Politics of Starvation, and the Loss of Aboriginal Life (Regina: University of Regina Press, 2013).

strands.title: Labour and the settler order
strands.focus: Integrates settler workers' ongoing appropriation of Indigenous land into Canadian working-class history.
strands.works: Fred Burrill, "The Settler Order Framework: Rethinking Canadian Working-Class History," Labour/Le Travail 83 (2019): 173–197.

strands.title: Critiques: fatalism, region, period, exploitation
strands.focus: From inside the theory, Macoun and Strakosch: SCT 'posits a structural inevitability', 'can depict colonization as structurally inevitable', risks 'colonial fatalism' and 'does not account for Indigenous lives'; yet 'the fact that settler colonialism struggles to narrate its own ending does not mean that it cannot end' (2013). Rowse: a 'teleology of elimination' (2014, abstract). Greer: one mode among several, dominant in some periods and regions (2019). Shoemaker: universal theory or English heritage? (2019). Englert: 'the elimination of the native … does not accurately define the overall logic of settler colonialism'; settler colonies in Africa and South America 'were built on the exploitation of indigenous peoples'; accumulation by dispossession 'carried out by all classes of settlers, including by workers' (2020, with Kelley and Speed 2017).
strands.works: Alissa Macoun and Elizabeth Strakosch, "The Ethical Demands of Settler Colonial Theory," Settler Colonial Studies 3, nos. 3–4 (2013): 426–443.; Tim Rowse, "Indigenous Heterogeneity," Australian Historical Studies 45, no. 3 (2014): 297–310.; Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Beyond," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association / Revue de la Société historique du Canada 30, no. 1 (2019): 61–86.; Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Empire in Early America," William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 383–390.; Nancy Shoemaker, "Settler Colonialism: Universal Theory or English Heritage?" William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 369–374.; Jeffrey Ostler and Nancy Shoemaker, "Settler Colonialism in Early American History: Introduction," William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 361–368.

strands.title: Indigenous studies and the field: who made it, whom it displaces
strands.focus: Kauanui: Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did', yet 'he tends to be most frequently cited as if he had'; 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies'; indigeneity is 'a category of analysis that is distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality'; Warrior counted ASA panels and feared the field had become 'an answer to the chronic need for more attention to … Native and Indigenous studies' (2016). Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel: the field 'can displace, overshadow, or even mask over Indigenous studies'; 'when settlers take up these questions, it's suddenly considered a legitimate field of study' (2014). Goeman answers from the same field: Wolfe 'critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner' and his work 'became a place to engage Indigenous studies concerns in relation to settler colonial studies' (2016). Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge the field (2019, abstract).
strands.works: Shino Konishi, "First Nations Scholars, Settler Colonial Studies, and Indigenous History," Australian Historical Studies 50, no. 3 (2019): 285–304.; J. Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).; Corey Snelgrove, Rita Kaur Dhamoon and Jeff Corntassel, "Unsettling Settler Colonialism: The Discourse and Politics of Settlers, and Solidarity with Indigenous Nations," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 3, no. 2 (2014): 1–32.

strands.title: Slavery and Black studies critiques
strands.focus: How settler-colonial and decolonial frameworks place slavery and Black people. Wolfe 2006 (read) sets out the opposed racialisations of Black and Indigenous people in the United States; Tuck and Yang's settler–native–slave triad (read) is what Garba and Sorentino answer. Both authors' words are now read; the critics' remain at abstract level.
strands.works: Tapji Garba and Sara-Maria Sorentino, "Slavery Is a Metaphor: A Critical Commentary on Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang's 'Decolonization Is Not a Metaphor'," Antipode 52, no. 3 (2020): 764–782.; Jared Sexton, "The Vel of Slavery: Tracking the Figure of the Unsovereign," Critical Sociology 42, nos. 4–5 (2016): 583–597.; Tiffany Lethabo King, The Black Shoals: Offshore Formations of Black and Native Studies (Durham: Duke University Press, 2019).

strands.title: Structure and its end: Wolfe and Veracini read together
strands.focus: Two emphases within one formula, not a documented exchange between opponents. Wolfe's structure is 'a continuity through time' that 'does not stop' with frontier homicide and 'has not been subject to election results' (2006). Veracini accepts the 'frequently quoted passage' and adds that 'the structure persistently pursues a specific end point' and 'extinguishes itself', so that settler colonialism 'covers its tracks' (2011): the end point is the settler project's attempted elimination of the settler–Indigenous relation, which Veracini distinguishes from decolonisation. The History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) records the two authors co-cited by 3.0% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, a readership pairing that does not itself establish a dispute. Englert reads both as drawing 'a sharp analytical separation' between eliminatory settler and exploitative franchise colonies and finds the separation does not fit Africa or South America (2020); Macoun and Strakosch find in the structure a 'colonial fatalism' and recall the label 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world' (2013): these readings establish different emphases placed on the same structure. Veracini's obituary records Wolfe as 'still a Marxist' of 'the young Marx' for whom 'things are not things in themselves but relationships' (2016).
strands.works: Wolfe, "Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native" (2006); Veracini, "Introducing settler colonial studies" (2011) and "Patrick Wolfe (1949–2016)" (2016); Macoun and Strakosch, "The Ethical Demands of Settler Colonial Theory" (2013); Englert, "Settlers, Workers, and the Logic of Accumulation by Dispossession" (2020).

strands.title: Canadian history beside and under the frame, 2009–2020
strands.focus: Works that Canadian PhDs read with Wolfe and Veracini, few of which adopt his vocabulary. Treaty history (Miller 2009, a distinctive riser among Canadian PhDs inside the Indigenous family in the 2026-10-23 release), racialisation and law in British Columbia's 'contact zone' (Mawani 2009), settler self-examination after residential schools (Regan 2010; Battell Lowman and Barker 2015: 'Canada and Settler Colonialism', 'It's Always All About the Land'), starvation policy (Daschuk 2013), Indigenous women's work 'in modern Native ways' (McCallum 2014), the TRC's finding that Canada's policy aimed 'to eliminate Aboriginal governments … and … cause Aboriginal peoples to cease to exist as distinct … entities' and 'can best be described as "cultural genocide"' (2015), imperial family and archive (Perry 2015), women homesteaders in 'the spadework of British colonialism' who 'took part in dispossessing Indigenous people' (Carter 2016), the settler-colonial city (Hugill 2017), the settler order in working-class history (Burrill 2019), Japanese Canadian dispossession (Stanger-Ross 2020), and Harris's reflections (2020). Veracini's own history says the Canadian historiography was 'late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis' (2013). Publisher descriptions, not the books, are read; none of Miller, Daschuk, McCallum, Perry 2015, Carter 2016 or Stanger-Ross uses the phrase on its page.
strands.works: Miller, Compact, Contract, Covenant (2009); Mawani, Colonial Proximities (2009); Regan, Unsettling the Settler Within (2010); Daschuk, Clearing the Plains (2013); McCallum, Indigenous Women, Work, and History (2014); Battell Lowman and Barker, Settler (2015); TRC, Honouring the Truth, Reconciling for the Future (2015); Perry, Colonial Relations (2015); Carter, Imperial Plots (2016); Hugill, "What Is a Settler-Colonial City?" (2017); Burrill, "The Settler Order Framework" (2019); Stanger-Ross, ed., Landscapes of Injustice (2020); Harris, A Bounded Land (2020).

strands.title: A field's institutions: journal, associations, memorials
strands.focus: NAISA founded 2008 after an ASA panel of 2002 asked whether American Studies could be 'an intellectual home' for Native studies (Kauanui). Settler Colonial Studies founded 2011 'in an open access format (entirely run on volunteer labour)' and moved to Taylor & Francis 'within two years' (Snelgrove et al.; Edmonds and Carey 2013). Wolfe edited paired issues of the journal and of AICRJ (2013) and answered the binary charge with The Settler Complex (2016). ASA 2015: Goldstein's reappraisal and Warrior's count of panels. Wolfe's death (18 February 2016) brought obituaries from the journal (Veracini), AICRJ (Goeman), Aboriginal History (Birch) and an American Quarterly forum (2017); a Festschrift followed (Race, Place, Trace, 2022).
strands.works: Kauanui (2016); Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014); Edmonds and Carey, "A New Beginning for Settler Colonial Studies" (2013); Wolfe, ed., "Recuperating Binarism" (2013) and The Settler Complex (2016); Veracini (2016); Goeman (2016); Birch (2016); American Quarterly 69:2 (2017); Slyomovics and Veracini, eds., Race, Place, Trace (2022).
